The Matthew Effect is a sociological phenomenon describing how well known researchers often receive disproportionately greater recognition than lesser known scientists, even when their contributions are comparable. The term was coined by sociologist Robert K. Merton in 1968 and derives its name from a biblical passage suggesting that those who already possess advantages tend to accumulate more over time.

In scientific communities, the Matthew Effect can influence funding decisions, citation counts, and professional opportunities. Established researchers often attract more attention, making their work more visible and likely to be cited. As a result, younger or less prominent scientists may struggle to gain recognition despite producing high quality research.

The concept has implications beyond academia. Similar patterns appear in business, education, and social media, where early success can generate further opportunities. Consequently, the Matthew Effect is frequently cited in discussions of inequality and meritocracy.
